'''''Taxodium ascendens''''', also known as '''pond cypress''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TAAS|taxon=Taxodium ascendens|access-date=8 December 2015}}</ref> is a [[deciduous]] [[conifer]] of the genus ''[[Taxodium]]'', native to [[North America]]. Many [[botanist]]s treat it as a [[variety (biology)|variety]] of bald cypress, ''[[Taxodium distichum]]'' (as ''T. distichum'' var. ''imbricatum'') rather than as a distinct [[species]], but it differs in [[habitat]], occurring mainly in still [[blackwater river]]s, ponds and [[Swamp|swamps]] without silt-rich flood deposits. It predominates in [[cypress dome]] habitats.

==Description==

''Taxodium ascendens'' is a medium-sized [[Conifer|deciduous conifer]] that is native to the southeastern [[United States]].''<ref name=":52">{{Cite web |title=USDA Plants Database |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=TAAS |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=plants.usda.gov}}</ref> Taxodium ascendens'' reaches on average {{convert|15|-|18|m}} in height. Pond cypress are typically between 50 – 85 ft tall and 15–30 ft wide.<ref name=":23">{{Cite web |title=Florida Native Plant Society (FNPS) |url=https://www.fnps.org/plant/taxodium-ascendens |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=www.fnps.org}}</ref> Compared to ''T. distichum'', the leaves are shorter (3–10 mm long), slenderer and are on shoots that tend to be erect rather than spreading. The trunk is expanded at the base, even on young trees, assisting the tree in anchoring in the soft, muddy soil. The [[conifer cone|cones]] also tend to be smaller, not over 2.5 cm diameter. The pond cypress leaves are more needle-shaped (like the shaft of an awl or a screwdriver), in a spiral arrangement that stays close to the stem.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-01 |title=Year of the Tree: Bald Cypress or Pond Cypress? {{!}} NC State Parks |url=https://www.ncparks.gov/state-parks/carvers-creek-state-park/news/september-2022-newsletter |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=www.ncparks.gov |language=en}}</ref> The leaves are deciduous, simple, alternate, awl-like needles. Its cones are round, ovulate, between {{convert|1/2|-|1+1/4|in|cm}} long.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=ENH-777/ST619: Taxodium ascendens: Pondcypress |url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/ST619 |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=edis.ifas.ufl.edu |language=en}}</ref> The bark is also a paler gray color. Cypresses are known for their prominent "knees" and buttressed trunks that define the species however ''Taxodium ascendens'' is less likely to have "knees" than ''Taxodium distichum''.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |last=Communications |first=IFAS |title=Pond Cypress - Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences - University of Florida, Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences - UF/IFAS |url=https://programs.ifas.ufl.edu/florida-4-h-forest-ecology/forest-ecology-contest/contest-stations/forest-ecosystems/freshwater-swamps/pond-cypress/ |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=programs.ifas.ufl.edu |language=en}}</ref> Like bald cypresses, pond cypresses growing in water have a characteristic growth trait called [[cypress knee]]s; these are woody projections called '[[pneumatophore]]s', which are sent above the water from the roots.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}Due to the dry nature of the habitat for the pond cypress, it has developed thicker, fire resistant bark.<ref name=":14"/>

==Distribution==
This species is native to the [[southeastern United States]], from southeastern [[Virginia]] to southeastern [[Louisiana]] and south into [[Florida]] except for the [[Florida Keys]].{{citation needed|date=March 2023}} Stunted individuals of pond cypress are notable in the dwarf cypress savanna of the [[Everglades National Park]].{{citation needed|date=March 2023}} ''Taxodium ascendens'' is most frequently found in the southeastern [[United States]] ranging from [[Virginia]] to [[Louisiana]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Taxodium ascendens, T. distichum |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/tree/taxspp/all.html |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=www.fs.usda.gov}}</ref>

==Habitat==
[[File:Taxodium ascendens in the Black Water, Okefenokee.jpg|thumb|''T. ascendens'' in [[Blackwater river|black water]], [[Okefenokee Swamp]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], USA]]
''Taxodium ascendens'' occurs naturally in shallow [[pond]]s, lake margins, [[swamp]]s and [[wetland]]s. It prefers wet, poorly drained and acidic soils, at an altitude of {{convert|0|-|30|m}} above sea level. The pond cypress preferred habitat is along the banks of ponds and lakes where the water is stagnant.<ref name=":03">{{Cite web |last=Milligan |first=Lara |date=2018-03-30 |title=The Great Cypress Debate |url=https://blogs.ifas.ufl.edu/pinellasco/2018/03/30/the-great-cypress-debate/ |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=UF/IFAS Extension Pinellas County |language=en}}</ref> This tree is native to southern swamps, [[bayou]]s and rivers, and is known to tolerate extended periods of intense flooding.<ref name=":42">{{Cite web |title=Taxodium distichum var. imbricarium (Pond Cypress) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/taxodium-distichum-var-imbricarium/ |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> Pond cypress are most frequently found in isolated depressions fed by nutrient-poor, shallow ground water.<ref name=":14"/> ''Taxodium ascendens'' grows easily in average, medium to wet, moisture-retentive but reasonably well-drained soils in full sun. It prefers moist, acidic, sandy soils, but tolerates a wide range of soil conditions ranging from average moisture soils to wet soils in standing water.<ref name=":42"/>

== Taxonomy ==
''Taxodium ascendens'' was discovered and identified by botanist [[Adolphe-Théodore Brongniart]] in 1833.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Taxodium ascendens Brongn. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:263754-1 |access-date=2023-12-05 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> The pond cypress is also known by other synonyms "''Taxodium'' ''distichum'' var. ''imbricatum'' (Nutt.) Croom"<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2022-01-07 |title=Taxodium distichum var. imbricarium x Taxodium muc |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1079/cabicompendium.52618 |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=CABI Compendium|doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.52618 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and "''Taxodium distichum'' var. ''ascendens'' (Brongn.) Mast."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Taxodium distichum var. ascendens {{!}} International Plant Names Index |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/77293088-1 |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=www.ipni.org}}</ref>

== Uses ==
''Taxodium ascendens'' is typically used for ornamental purposes or decoration in more urban environments unlike the bald cypress which can be used in heavy duty construction.<ref name=":23"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Bald Cypress (Taxodium distichum) |url=https://tpwd.texas.gov/huntwild/wild/species/baldcypress/#:~:text=Bald%20cypress%20is%20used%20for,,%20canoes,%20and%20ceremonial%20objects. |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=tpwd.texas.gov}}</ref> Pond cypress are also used in wetland restoration and enhancement.<ref name=":23"/>

== Ecology ==
Like many other large semiaquatic plants, ''Taxodium ascendens'' roots and trunk provides structural complexity to shelter to young aquatic animals such as the larvae of [[amphibian]]s and juvenile fish. Specifically the endangered flatwoods salamander will only lay their eggs in dry ponds populated with ''Taxodium ascendens''.<ref name=":14"/>

''Taxodium ascendens'' is susceptible to fires during the drier arid seasons where ponds lose the majority of their water but these trees have developed a thicker bark to better survive these conditions.<ref name=":52"/>

== Etymology ==
The varietal name "imbricatum" means overlapping, in reference to the manner in which the leaves lie on the twigs.<ref name=":03"/> The term “ascendens” suggests the leaves that point or grow upward in an arching or curving fashion.<ref name=":03"/>

== Conservation status ==
The pond cypress is considered "apparently secure" (S4) in [[North Carolina]], "critically imperiled" (S1) in [[Virginia]], and "exotic" in [[Delaware]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=NatureServe Explorer 2.0 |url=https://explorer.natureserve.org/Taxon/ELEMENT_GLOBAL.2.686969/Taxodium_ascendens_-_Woodwardia_virginica_Swamp_Woodland |access-date=2023-11-15 |website=explorer.natureserve.org}}</ref>
